subtype: Approach: deciding purpose and audience first [Thinking]
passage:
When I made my art account last year, the first thing I did wasn't posting. I'm Sarita, and I sat on the stairs with my phone and asked myself: why am I doing this?
To get famous? No, that made my stomach knot. To sell drawings? Not yet. The honest answer was that I wanted Nani in Jaipur and my cousins to see what I make, and maybe a few friends from school to say something nice.
Once I knew that, the rest was easy. If the audience is family and friends, the account should be private. So I set it to private and only accepted people I actually know. My brother Santosh said I'd never get followers that way. I said, “I don't want followers. I want Nani.”
It also changed what I post: finished pieces and messy sketches, but no selfies, no school uniform, nothing about where we live.

qa.q: Who did Sarita want to see the art?
qa.a: Nani in Jaipur, the cousins, and a few friends from school.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel about the idea of getting famous?
qa.a: It made Sarita's stomach knot, a sign of discomfort with a big public audience.

qa.q: What else could Sarita decide as the account grows?
qa.a: Review every few months whether the purpose has changed, say toward selling, and adjust privacy only after talking it over with family.

qa.q: How does Santosh see the private account?
qa.a: Santosh thinks it limits followers, not seeing that Sarita's purpose is family, not fame.

grounding: Shows a teen asking why to post at all, choosing to share art with family and friends only, and setting the account to private so the purpose shapes what goes up.

subtype: Approach: deciding purpose and audience first [Thinking]

Art teacher's note, Tuesday
Kashish asked me after class whether she should put her sketches online, because her friend Tanuja has a public account with thousands of followers. Instead of answering, I asked her why she wanted to post at all.
She thought for a while. Then she said the truth was that she wanted her grandparents in Shillong to see her progress, and a few classmates who like drawing. Not strangers. Not numbers.
Once she had said it aloud, she worked out the rest herself: if that's the audience, the account should be private, and she would accept only people she knows. She also decided not to post her face or anything showing the school, since that doesn't serve the purpose.
She set it up on her phone before leaving the art room. I suggested she show her parents the settings tonight. Next week I will ask how her grandparents liked the first sketch.

qa.q: Where do Kashish's grandparents live?
qa.a: In Shillong.

qa.q: What did Kashish want most from posting, once she thought about it?
qa.a: Kashish wanted her grandparents and a few classmates to see her progress, and felt uninterested in strangers or numbers.

qa.q: What else could Kashish do to keep the account true to its purpose?
qa.a: Check followers now and then, removing anyone she doesn't know, and keep showing her parents the settings.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's public account differ from Kashish's plan?
qa.a: Tanuja's account seeks many followers, while Kashish's aims at a small, known audience, so they suit different purposes.

grounding: A teacher notes a teen asking why she wants to post, choosing family and a few classmates as her audience, and setting her art account to private.

subtype: Approach: thinking before posting with a simple test [Thinking]
passage:
In their town of Nagaur, the school bus had broken down for the third time that month, and Gautam had walked four kilometres in the heat. That evening, on the family phone, he typed a long post: the bus contractor was a thief, the principal didn't care, the whole school was a joke.
His thumb hovered over the button. Then he remembered what his cousin Parveen had taught him: before you post anything, picture three people reading it. A teacher. Ammi. Someone who might hire you one day.
He pictured Sharma Sir reading “the whole school is a joke”. His face went warm. He pictured Ammi, who knew the contractor's wife from the mandir. Then a stranger in an office years from now, scrolling.
He deleted the post. Instead, with two other students, he wrote a short, polite letter about the bus, and they gave it to Sharma Sir the next morning.

qa.q: How far did Gautam walk in the heat?
qa.a: Four kilometres.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he typed the post?
qa.a: Gautam was angry and exhausted after the long walk, frustrated at the third breakdown.

qa.q: Why was the polite letter a better choice than the post?
qa.a: It raised the real problem with someone who could act, without words he'd regret teachers, family or employers seeing.

qa.q: How might Sharma Sir have reacted to the post, compared with the letter?
qa.a: The post would likely have hurt and angered him; the letter lets him take the complaint seriously.

grounding: Shows a student picturing a teacher, a parent and a future employer reading an angry post, deleting it, and raising the complaint properly instead.

subtype: Approach: audit of privacy settings and old posts [Action]
passage:
I'm Salma. Vasudha and I were on her bed on Sunday afternoon when she said, “I'm doing a clean-up,” and turned her phone so I could watch.
She went through her account like a detective. First the tags: she removed herself from two group photos someone else had posted publicly. Then settings: she switched on approval for tags, so nobody can tag her without her saying yes. Then location: she turned off location sharing on the app and on her camera too, so photos wouldn't carry it.
Then she scrolled right back to Class Seven. There was an old post of her at the school gate, in uniform, with the school's name clear on the board behind her. She stared at it for a moment and deleted it. “Anyone could work out where I am at eight every morning,” she said.
It took about forty minutes. She looked relieved when she was done, I think.

qa.q: What did the old post show?
qa.a: Vasudha at the school gate, in uniform, with the school's name clear on the board behind her.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha delete the Class Seven post?
qa.a: She felt uneasy seeing how clearly it showed her routine, worried anyone could work out where she is at eight every morning.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha add to the clean-up?
qa.a: Show a parent the new settings, and repeat the check every few months, since old posts and new tags pile up.

qa.q: How does the clean-up look to Salma?
qa.a: Salma sees a careful, detective-like check and thinks Vasudha looked relieved, though Salma can't be sure.

grounding: A friend watches a teen review tags, location sharing and public photos, delete an old post showing her school gate and uniform, and switch off location.

subtype: Approach: setting time boundaries for use [Action]
passage:
Dear Bidisha,
You asked why I've been so slow replying lately. It's not you, I promise. I've changed how I use social media, and I want to explain before you think I'm ignoring you.
I noticed I was checking it about forty times a day, even in the middle of maths homework. It was in charge of me, instead of me being in charge of it. So now I have two windows: 7:30 to 8 in the evening, and fifteen minutes after lunch on weekends. That's when I check, reply and post. I've turned off all notifications except calls, so the phone doesn't pull at me in between.
During exam weeks I'm nearly offline. Just the class group once a day for homework updates.
It felt strange at first. Now I actually like knowing I'll see everything at 7:30.
So if I don't reply for a few hours, I'm not upset. I'll get back to you at 7:30.
Jeevan

qa.q: When is Jeevan's evening window?
qa.a: 7:30 to 8 in the evening.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel about the new routine now?
qa.a: Jeevan felt strange at first, but now enjoys it and feels in control rather than pulled.

qa.q: What else could Jeevan add to make the windows easier to keep?
qa.a: Keep the phone in another room outside the windows, so there's no temptation to check early.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel after reading the letter?
qa.a: Bidisha would likely feel reassured that the slow replies aren't personal, and maybe curious to try it.

grounding: Shows a student limiting social media to two windows a day, turning off notifications and staying nearly offline in exam weeks so it serves the student.

subtype: Approach: setting time boundaries for use [Action]
passage:
Hemant, you asked how I stopped my phone eating my evenings. I'm Chetan, and it was one rule, really: two windows.
I used to check everything every few minutes: likes, comments, the group chats. I'd sit down to study, look up, and it would be eleven. So in January I decided social media gets two slots a day. Twenty minutes after school, around 4:30, and twenty minutes after dinner. That's it. Everything else waits.
Then I turned off notifications for everything except calls and Mummy. That was the big one, honestly. If the phone doesn't buzz, you don't think about it.
And exam weeks: almost nothing. I told my friends, “I'm off till the 20th, message Mummy if it's urgent.”
Did I miss stuff? Some memes. Nobody died. My marks went up a bit, but mostly I just feel less jittery. Like my time is mine again.

qa.q: How does Chetan feel since the change?
qa.a: Chetan feels less jittery, as if the time belongs to Chetan again.

qa.q: What else could Chetan try if the two windows start stretching?
qa.a: Set a timer for each twenty-minute slot, so it ends on time even when the feed is interesting.

qa.q: How might Chetan's friends see the exam-week rule?
qa.a: They might miss Chetan in the chats at first, but knowing to message Mummy if urgent makes it easy to accept.

subtype: Approach: chasing likes and followers [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Parul Didi,
You asked why I deleted my account. I'll tell you properly.
In the summer I wanted followers. I had 180, and a boy in my class had 3,000 from doing stunts. So I started posting stunts too: a backflip off the park bench, then off the wall by the water tank, each one a bit higher, because the higher ones got more likes.
And I got hooked on the number. If a video got 400 likes, I felt great. If the next got 90, I felt awful all evening, refreshing and refreshing. My whole mood depended on people I don't even know.
Then in August I slipped on the wall and landed badly on my wrist. Papa found the videos while we waited at the clinic. He wasn't angry, just scared, and that scared me. We sat together that night and I deleted the account.
My wrist is fine now. My head feels quieter too.
Uday

qa.q: How many followers did Uday have at the start of the summer?
How did Uday feel when a video got only 90 likes?
qa.a: Uday felt awful all evening, anxious and refreshing again and again.

qa.q: What could Uday have done instead of chasing likes?
qa.a: Posted for friends Uday actually knows, and tried backflips only with a trained coach, so neither mood nor safety depended on strangers.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt finding the videos at the clinic?
qa.a: Papa was scared more than angry, realising how much risk Uday had been taking for likes.

grounding: Shows a teen posting ever more daring stunt videos to gain followers, feeling anxious when likes drop, and finding that mood rides on numbers nobody can control.

Jagdish, you asked why I went quiet online. I'm Chaitanya, and it's a bit embarrassing.
Last year I started chasing followers. I noticed my photos near the edge of the old fort wall got far more likes than normal ones. So every weekend I went back and posted something more daring: sitting on the edge, then standing, then one foot out for the camera.
The numbers became everything. A good post, and I'd be happy all day. A flop, and I'd feel sick, checking every five minutes, wondering what was wrong with me. I didn't control those numbers, but they controlled me.
It stopped when a guard at the fort caught me on the wall, pulled me down, and phoned my mother right there. She came straight away. She didn't shout. She just held on to my arm the whole way home.

In Mexico City, the summer holidays were hot and ordinary for Rosa: helping at her aunt's bakery, reading on the roof, the park on Sundays. Then she'd open her phone. Layla, a girl from her class, was on a white beach in Cancún. Someone else was at a concert. An influencer she'd never met was having breakfast in Paris.
By August she felt her whole life was grey. She stopped wanting to go to the park. “Nothing I do is worth a photo,” she told her aunt.
Her aunt laughed gently and showed Rosa her own phone: a photo of the bakery's best cake, taken on the one day it didn't crack. “That's what people post. The one good day.”
That night Rosa went through the accounts she followed and unfollowed forty, the ones that left her feeling small. She kept her friends, a baking channel and a comic artist. By the next week she was back on the roof with a book, and it felt fine again.

qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: How did Rosa feel about her summer by August?
qa.a: Rosa felt left out and low, sure her grey life held nothing worth a photo.

qa.q: What else could Rosa do when the comparisons creep back?

In the girls' hostel of their boarding school in Dehradun, Sunday evening was phone hour, and Bidisha spent all of it scrolling. Classmates at home on leave were posting a family trip to the hills, a new dress, a birthday dinner somewhere fancy. Bidisha, in the hostel because her parents couldn't travel that month, felt more and more left out.
By the third Sunday she didn't want to go to the common-room games at all. Nitin, the house counsellor, noticed her sitting alone and asked what was wrong.
“Everyone's life looks so good,” she said.
“Everyone posts their best ten minutes,” Nitin said. “Nobody posts the car-sickness on the hill road.” He asked her which accounts left her feeling worse. She scrolled and counted; most were people she barely knew.
She unfollowed them right there in the counsellor's room. The next Sunday she spent half the phone hour on a call with her mother and the other half at carrom.

subtype: Approach: accepting requests from strangers [Pitfall]
passage:
In Class Eight I accepted every follow request, even from people I'd never heard of. I'm Simran, and I thought a big number made me look popular. My brother Suraj said it was a bad idea. I ignored him.
Most of those accounts never did anything. Then one of them started messaging me: friendly at first, liking every post, asking about my favourite singer. After a week the questions changed. Which school? Which bus? What time do you get home? Then: “Don't tell your parents we talk, they won't understand.”
That line gave me a cold feeling in my stomach. I didn't reply. I walked straight into the kitchen and showed Mummy the whole chat. She took screenshots with me, reported the account and blocked it, and that evening we went through my followers together and removed everyone I didn't actually know.
I have eighty-four followers now. I know every one of them.

qa.q: How many followers does Simran have now?
qa.a: Eighty-four.

qa.q: How did Simran feel reading "Don't tell your parents we talk"?
qa.a: Simran felt a cold, frightened feeling, sensing the secrecy was a warning sign.

qa.q: What should Simran do if a similar request comes again?
qa.a: Decline follows from strangers, and if anyone asks for secrecy or personal details, stop replying and tell a parent at once.

qa.q: How might Suraj see what happened?
qa.a: Suraj was right that accepting strangers was risky, and is probably relieved Simran told Mummy straight away.

grounding: Shows a teen accepting strangers' follows to look popular, then getting messages pressing for personal details and secrecy, and telling a parent and blocking the account.

Parent's note, Wednesday night
Tonight Rashmi came to me with her phone, looking frightened. For months she has accepted almost every follow request, to look popular; I had not known. Tonight one of those strangers sent her a private message asking for her address “to send a gift”, her school's name and a photo, and saying, “Keep this between us.”
She had not replied. I told her she had done exactly the right thing by coming to me. We took screenshots, reported the account and blocked it together. Her brother Vishal, who knows the settings better than I do, helped her make the account private and remove every follower she does not know in person. It came down from over nine hundred to about a hundred.
She was quiet for a while, then said, “I thought it made me look popular.” Tomorrow I will tell her class teacher, so the school can remind all the students.

qa.a: Rashmi looked frightened, unsettled by the message and the request to keep it secret.

I'm Nirmala, and I was sitting with Jahnavi on the school bus when the comment came in under her dance video: “lol who told you that you can dance.” I saw her face drop. Her thumbs were already moving to reply.
Then she stopped, locked the phone and put it in her bag. “Not now,” she said, mostly to herself. “An hour.”
She talked to me about the maths test for the rest of the ride, though she kept glancing at the bag. At home, about an hour later, she messaged me: “Checked again. Not replying. It's someone I don't even know.” She had deleted the comment and blocked the account.
That evening she called me, just to talk. She asked if I thought the video was bad. I said no, and meant it. She laughed a little and said she would post the next one anyway.
I don't know what she'd have typed on the bus. I'm glad she didn't.

Then our school robotics club needed a way to show our work. I asked Mrs Kulkarni, our club teacher, if we could make a page. She said yes, with rules: no faces without permission, no school address, and she'd be an admin too. So we did.
We post one build every week. Last month a college robotics team commented on our line-follower and offered a video call to help with the sensor. We did the call in the lab, with Mrs Kulkarni there.
So my phone isn't just for scrolling now. It's a kind of second classroom.

subtype: Approach: resetting after a regret [Revision]

Ojas had posted it at eleven at night in their Hyderabad flat, still angry after the cricket match: a photo of Disha dropping the catch that lost them the game, captioned “thanks for nothing, butterfingers”.
By morning it had thirty laughing reactions, and Disha hadn't come to the bus stop.
He looked at the post again in daylight and felt sick. She was the one who had stayed late every day to help him with his bowling. He deleted it before the bus arrived.
At school he found her in the library. “I posted that because I was angry, and it was cruel. I'm sorry. I've deleted it.” She didn't smile, but she nodded.
That evening he wrote a rule on a sticky note and stuck it on the back of his phone: If I'm upset, I don't post. I wait till morning.
Two weeks later, after another bad loss, he looked at the sticky note and put the phone down.

qa.a: If I'm upset, I don't post. I wait till morning.

grounding: Shows a teen who posted something unkind in anger deleting it, apologising to the person, and setting a rule not to post when upset.

subtype: Approach: resetting after a regret [Revision]
passage:
“Gargi, wait. Can I say something?”
“If it's about the post, I've seen it, Yusuf. Everyone has.”
“I deleted it this morning.”
“After a hundred people saw it.”
“I know.” He took a breath. “I was angry that you got the lead in the play and I didn't. I posted that stupid thing about your voice at midnight. It was mean, and it wasn't even true. I'm sorry.”
Gargi looked at him for a long moment. “It really hurt, you know.”
“I know. I'm not asking you to be fine with it.”
“Okay.” A pause. “Thanks for saying it to my face.”
“And I've made a rule. If I'm angry, the phone goes in the drawer till morning. No posting.”
“Does it work?”
“Ask me in a month.”
Gargi almost smiled. “I will."

qa.q: Why was Yusuf angry, by his own account?
qa.a: Gargi got the lead in the play and Yusuf didn't.

qa.q: How did Yusuf seem to feel while apologising?
qa.a: Yusuf seemed ashamed and nervous, taking a breath before admitting the post was mean and untrue.

qa.q: What else could Yusuf do to back up the apology?
qa.a: Keep the drawer rule, and perhaps say something kind about Gargi's role where the class can see it.

qa.q: How does the apology land for Gargi?
qa.a: Gargi is still hurt, but appreciates being told face to face, and is willing to see if Yusuf changes.

grounding: Shows a teen who posted something unkind in anger deleting it, apologising face to face, and setting a rule not to post while upset.
